meta.title: Somali A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 439 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Somali → English (see the Somali, recall the meaning) and English → Somali (see an English meaning, recall the Somali). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 439 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. A2 WAS PLANNED AT 500 WORDS AND HOLDS 439: after A1, that is every word English Wiktionary has that the Somali Wikipedia uses at all and that is not a variant spelling, a definite form filed as a word, or a slur; padding to the plan would teach the noise. The last words dealt appear in only one or two articles, so their order says little. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Somali, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 254 of the 439 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the months, the seasons and the times of day, directions and places, clothes, work and jobs, people and the stages of life, feelings, travel, the land and the weather, animals, the body and health, food and the kitchen, the things of a home, talking and learning, the verbs of doing, describing people and things, the faith and the feasts, the ordinals, and the little words of time — and the other 185 are the commonest remaining words of the Somali Wikipedia (its articles of 150 words or more), each counted over its forms, since Somali writes the article and the endings onto the word (buugga 'the book', cunay 'ate'). The corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (places, history, government), and the cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. THE SOURCES ARE THIN: English Wiktionary has about a thousand Somali words and lacks some of the commonest (tag 'go', lacag 'money', hadda 'now'), so 88 of the 439 are glossed by Folio itself with the standard meaning a course or dictionary gives. Words are written in the ordinary Somali spelling, which marks no tone; under 64 of them is the accented spelling English Wiktionary gives (nín 'man', gabádh 'girl'), the accent marking the high tone that tells, for instance, a masculine noun from a feminine one. Folio's own glosses carry none, since an accent from memory would be a claim with no source. A noun's gender is in its label and its plural is given with the plural's own gender, which is often the other one (wiil 'boy' is masculine, wiilal 'boys' feminine). The Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters, among them c, x, q, dh and the long vowels. Example sentences are few: 7 of the 439 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 125 Somali sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Somali voice, and one without it would read the word in another language's sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, accents, genders and plurals: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0), and Folio's own glosses for the words it lacks. Frequency: the Somali Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
